1.pericope_label: The writing of divorcement; she may not return to her former husband
debates: What the uncleanness is that grounds the permission: Henry holds it must be something less than adultery, since for that the woman was to die, and less than the suspicion of it, since for that there were the waters of jealousy, but that it must be something, a cause shown and not a mere dislike; Clarke takes the opposite view and rests it on practice rather than the word, that any cause of dislike will do since it is certain a Jew might put away his wife for any cause that seemed good to him; Wesley stands between, allowing a distemper of body or quality of mind not observed before marriage, or some light carriage, but nothing amounting to adultery

Whether the woman is absolutely or relatively defiled: Clarke reads it absolutely, that God counted all such after-marriages pollution, which is the ground on which our Lord argues that whoever marries the woman put away commits adultery, and that nothing but adultery can be a legal cause of separation on either side; Wesley denies the absolute sense, that she is not defiled as though her second marriage were itself a sin, but only with respect to her first husband, to whom she is now among forbidden things

What standing the permission has: Henry calls it the permission the Pharisees erroneously cited as a precept and Wesley distinguishes it from both a command and an approbation; Calvin goes furthest, that divorce was never in accordance with the Law at all, being directly repugnant to the first institution of God, and that the Jews concluded improperly from their impunity that what God did not punish was lawful
outliers: Calvin's argument from the closeness of the bond, that God declared the tie between husband and wife closer than that between parent and child, so that if a son cannot shake off the paternal yoke no cause can dissolve a marriage
Henry's observation that divorce was probably in use before this, being taken for granted in Leviticus, so that Moses gave rules for a thing already practised

Keil's derivation of the Hebrew term as a hewing or cutting off from the man with whom the wife was to be one flesh, and his suggestion that the custom of such letters was adopted in Egypt, where writing had found its way into all the relations of life

Keil's account of what the fourth verse accomplishes, that since the custom could not be abolished outright, the impossibility of reunion would put a check upon frivolous divorces that a prohibition could not

Clarke's printing of a full specimen bill of divorcement from Maimonides and Bartolocci, with its dating from the creation of the world and its clauses for any other name the parties or their cities might bear
Clarke's inference from the Gospels that the wife had as much right to put away her husband as the husband had to put away his wife

5.pericope_label: The new husband free for one year; the millstone; manstealing; the plague of leprosy
debates: What the command about leprosy requires: Keil rejects the received reading, that when signs appeared they were to do whatever the priests directed, on two grounds, that the appeal to Miriam does not fit since she brought leprosy on herself by rebelling against Moses rather than by opposing the priests, and that the reading cannot be reconciled with the Hebrew construction; Ellicott takes the point to be social rather than procedural, that a leader of Israel was shut out of the camp seven days so that no relaxation could be allowed for great or wealthy persons; Calvin dismisses two other readings, the allegorists and those who make it a merely sanitary commandment, the latter of which he calls poor and almost unmeaning

Why Miriam is remembered: Keil makes the reference an argument against the priestly-obedience reading, since her leprosy followed rebellion against Moses; Ellicott makes it an argument against exemption for the great, since she was treated by the strict letter; Gill makes it a warning against entertaining evil suspicions of those in authority and speaking evil of them
Who the new wife is: Gill records that Jarchi takes her for a widow and the Targum of Jonathan for a virgin, and observes that the term excepts a divorced wife taken back, who cannot be called new
outliers: Calvin's remark that God's permitting a bride to enjoy herself with her husband is no trifling proof of his indulgence, since the connection cannot but be affected with some amount of sin, which God not only pardons but covers with the veil of holy matrimony
Clarke's parallel from outside Israel, that Alexander ordered the soldiers who had married that year to spend the winter with their wives while the army lay in quarters
Ellicott's philological note that he shall not go forth in warfare nor shall warfare pass upon him in any form, the service of the tabernacle being itself called a warfare
Ellicott's structural observation that the word rendered a man's life is literally a soul, and that this word joins the law of the millstone to the law of manstealing that follows
Calvin's extension of the millstone rule to every instrument a workman cannot do without, the husbandman's plough or spade or harrow, or a shoemaker's or potter's shop emptied
Calvin's ground for equating manstealing with murder, that the condition of slaves was so wretched that liberty was more than half of life, so that to take it away was almost to destroy the man

10.pericope_label: Thou shalt stand abroad; deliver him the pledge again when the sun goeth down
debates: What use a pledge can be that must be returned every night: Clarke puts the objection sharply, that the law would seem to preclude pledging altogether in the case of the abjectly poor, since no one would take in the morning what he must restore at night, and answers it himself by daily renewal, the creditor resuming his claim each morning and so keeping up his property until the debt was discharged; Gill reports the quite different answer the Jews gave, that the profit of the pledge was to exempt the debt from release in the seventh year and to prevent the borrower disposing of the goods to his children, payment being made from the pledge after his death

Why the creditor must wait outside: Calvin makes it a restraint on rapacity, since the avaricious rich given the run of a house would be satisfied with no moderation but would seize whatever was best, or would fill the wretched with rebuke and shame by contemptuously refusing this and that; Wesley names two motives rather than one, sparing the poor man the reproach of having his wants exposed and sparing the creditor the greediness the sight of the goods would stir in him

What the lender gains by obedience: Wesley takes the blessing literally as the poor man’s prayer and adds the distinction that although such a man’s prayers, if he be not himself good, will not avail for his own behalf, they will nevertheless avail for the benefit of the one who returned his cloak; Keil treats the closing clause as a formula used elsewhere in the book and lets it stand without expansion
outliers: Calvin's picture of what the other rule would license, the creditor ransacking his brother's house as though making an assault upon the very entrails of the poor
Wesley's note that the choice of pledge belongs to the borrower, provided what he brings is sufficient for the purpose
Keil's supply of the fact that makes the law necessary, that the poor man very often had nothing to pledge but the upper garment in which he slept
Gill's observation that the hour of return followed the kind of pledge, a night covering being restored at sunset and day clothes in the morning
Clarke's historical note that the Jews in several cases acted contrary to this rule and are cuttingly reproved for it by the prophet Amos
Calvin's list of what may never be taken back at all, the bed a man sleeps on, his coverlet, or his cloak, lest he be so stripped as to suffer from cold
themes: the borrower brings out the pledge
it shall be righteousness unto thee

14.pericope_label: Thou shalt not oppress an hired servant; every man shall die for his own sin
debates: How the rule squares with God visiting iniquity to the third and fourth generation: Calvin raises the objection himself and answers that God is a law unto himself, that he does not rush by blind impulse to vengeance so as to confound the innocent with the reprobate, but visits the fathers’ iniquity upon the children in such a way as to temper extreme severity with the greatest equity; Wesley answers it differently, granting that God does so visit but denying that he suffers men to do so, and then admitting a class of exceptions Calvin does not name, cases where the sovereign Lord of life and death has himself commanded it

Whether Achan is a counter-instance to the rule: Wesley cites the destruction of Achan’s household as precisely one of the commanded exceptions; Ellicott treats Achan, who perished not alone in his iniquity, as falling under a different head altogether rather than as an exception to this precept

What the clause about setting the heart on the wages means: Keil takes it as a longing, that the man lifts up his soul to his hire, and gathers the idiom from the Psalms, Hosea and Jeremiah; Calvin’s own version has the man sustaining his life by the wage, with the alternatives set beside it that he lifteth his soul unto it, that he pants for it, and that he hopes for and desires it for the maintenance of his life; Clarke fills the phrase with observation rather than philology
outliers: Henry's widening of the oppression beyond wages, to overloading with work, undue and unreasonable rebukes, and withholding proper maintenance, and his summary that masters should not be tyrants to their servants, for their Master is in heaven
Gill's citation of the Jerusalem Targum that the hire is not to be detained by force, with his own addition that neither may it be detained by fraud
Clarke's observation that the poor servant who seldom sees money yet finds from his master's affluence that money procures every comfort, and so longs for the day of payment

Keil's note that the command was needed to prevent an abusive transfer into human courts of what belongs to the movements of divine justice, the practice being common among the Persians and Macedonians
Calvin's appeal to natural common sense, that it is an act of barbarous madness to put children to death out of hatred to their father

Ellicott's history of the precept's observance and neglect, that Amaziah the son of Joash is specially noted in both Kings and Chronicles for keeping it, and that the Persians did not keep it with Daniel's accusers
themes: at his day give him his hire
every man for his own sin

17.pericope_label: Judgment of the stranger and fatherless; the forgotten sheaf and the gleanings
debates: Whose the leavings of the harvest are: Clarke states the case in terms of ownership, that the corners of the field, the gleanings and the forgotten sheaf were all the property of the poor, a principle the Hebrews extended to any produce forgotten at the general ingathering; Calvin will not go so far and hedges the duty on both sides, denying that God requires the wealthy to give so profusely as to despoil themselves, citing Paul’s measure that relief of the poor should not bring the distributing rich into distress, and denying equally that God absolutely assigns to the poor whatever remains as though they might seize it as their own

What the prohibition on taking a widow’s raiment covers: Wesley alone qualifies it, holding that what may not be pledged is the clothing she has daily and necessary use of, as being poor, and that the rule does not concern rich persons or superfluous raiment; Keil states the prohibition without that limitation

Why the memory of Egypt is invoked: Gill takes it as a producer of fellow-feeling, that the remembrance may cause sympathy with persons in distress; Clarke turns it into a warning about wealth, that those who have risen from penury ought to remember what their fears and anxieties were; Keil treats it as the formal ground of the section, repeated from an earlier chapter
outliers: Gill's reason for the special charge to judges, that the stranger and the fatherless are unable to defend themselves and have few if any to take their part
Clarke's observation that most people of affluence rose from comparative penury, since those born to estates frequently squander them

Clarke's proverb, that want of attention to this precept is why pride and arrogance mark those who have risen from poverty, and that their conduct gave rise to the saying that a beggar set on horseback will ride to the devil
Calvin's ground for the duty, that when God's bounty is exercised before our eyes it invites us to imitate him, and that it is ingratitude to withhold unkindly what we derive from his blessing
Calvin's citation of Paul's measure, that the relief of the poor should not bring the distributing rich themselves into distress

Gill's agricultural note that the olive was beaten with sticks and staves and that the grapes were gathered at much the same season, both after the wheat harvest about the end of June, those countries being more forward
themes: thou wast a bondman in Egypt
